name: Chlormadinone acetate pill
lead: Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin with antiandrogenic activity, used in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol such as Belara, which is sold in Germany and Brazil.[1] Because it blocks androgen receptors and lowers LH and FSH, such pills are used in some countries for androgen-related skin conditions including acne and hirsutism.[1]

Published trial information specific to acne is limited in the material reviewed. Registered studies compare body-weight change on Belara versus a drospirenone pill and examine hormonal contraceptives in polycystic ovary syndrome, but neither is an acne trial.[2][3]
infobox: Prescription only; not marketed in the US, UK, Canada or Australia

paras: Combined with ethinylestradiol, CMA is used for contraception and is also described as used for acne, hirsutism and other androgen-dependent conditions.[1] It is widely available in combined pills across much of Europe, Latin America and parts of Asia, but is not marketed in the US, UK, Canada or Australia.[1]

CMA is an androgen receptor antagonist with about 30 to 40 percent of the receptor affinity of cyproterone acetate, and acts as a weak partial agonist. It also suppresses LH and FSH, lowering testosterone and estradiol.[1]

CMA was discovered in 1959 and introduced medically in 1965. Eli Lilly marketed it in the US until 1971, and it was withdrawn in several countries around 1970 after mammary tumors appeared in beagle dogs at high doses; later research found no comparable risk in humans.[1]

At low dose with ethinylestradiol, reported effects include menstrual irregularities, headache, nausea, breast tenderness and vaginal discharge. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, and in menopausal therapy combined with estrogen it has been linked to increased breast cancer risk.[1]

No acne-specific trials were found. Registered studies include a phase 4 comparison of body-weight change during contraception with Belara versus Yasmin (n=100) and a study of the safety of hormonal contraceptive therapies in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (n=75).[2][3]

timeline.event: Withdrawn in several countries after dog mammary tumor findings.[1]

card.summary: A European antiandrogenic progestin in combined birth-control pills, used for acne in some countries with little published acne-specific trial data found.
card.note: Prescription-only; not sold in the US, UK, Canada or Australia.

quick.overview:
Chlormadinone acetate is a progestin with antiandrogen activity, combined with ethinylestradiol in pills such as Belara. It is used for contraception and for androgen-related skin conditions in countries where it is sold.

No acne-specific trials turned up in the sources reviewed; registered studies concern weight change and PCOS.
quick.mechanism: It blocks androgen receptors (about 30 to 40 percent of cyproterone acetate affinity) and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering testosterone.
quick.risks: Menstrual irregularity, headache, nausea and breast tenderness; contraindicated in pregnancy. Prescription only and unavailable in several countries including the US.
